title: Python Basics
subtitle: Your First Steps in Programming
description: Learn the fundamentals of Python programming from scratch. This course covers variables, control flow, functions, and lists — everything you need to start writing your own programs.

modules.title: What is Python & How to Set It Up
modules.content:
Why Python?

Python is one of the most popular programming languages in the world. It's known for being easy to read and beginner-friendly. If you've ever wanted to learn programming, Python is a fantastic place to start.

Python is used everywhere — from building websites, automating boring tasks, analyzing data, to creating AI models. Many companies in the Philippines and around the world use Python for their projects.

Installing Python

Go to python.org/downloads and download the latest version. During installation, make sure to check the box that says "Add Python to PATH" — this is important!

After installing, open your terminal (Command Prompt on Windows, Terminal on Mac/Linux) and type:

python --version

You should see something like Python 3.12.0. That means it's working!

Your First Program

Open any text editor (VS Code is recommended — it's free) and create a file called hello.py. Type this:

print("Hello, Kumusta!")

Save the file, then run it in your terminal:

python hello.py

Congratulations! You just wrote your first program. The print() function displays text on the screen.

How Python Works

Python reads your code line by line, from top to bottom. Each line is called a statement. Python is an interpreted language, which means it runs your code directly without compiling it first — making it super convenient for quick testing.

Think of Python like a recipe: it follows each instruction step by step, in order.
objectives: Understand what Python is and why it's popular
Write and run your first Python program
Understand how Python executes code line by line

modules.title: Variables & Data Types
modules.content:
What Are Variables?

Variables are like labeled containers that store data. You give a name to a value so you can use it later.

name = "Maria"
age = 25
height = 5.4
is_student = True

Here, name, age, height, and is_student are all variables.

Data Types

Python has several built-in data types:

  • String (str) — text, wrapped in quotes: "Hello" or 'Hello'
  • Integer (int) — whole numbers: 42, -7, 0
  • Float — decimal numbers: 3.14, 99.9
  • Boolean (bool) — True or False

Working with Strings

You can combine (concatenate) strings using the + operator:

first_name = "Juan"
last_name = "Dela Cruz"
full_name = first_name + " " + last_name
print(full_name)  # Output: Juan Dela Cruz

You can also use f-strings for cleaner formatting:

price = 150
print(f"The item costs ₱{price}")  # Output: The item costs ₱150

Type Conversion

Sometimes you need to convert between types:

age_str = "25"
age_num = int(age_str)   # Convert string to integer
price = float(100)       # Convert int to float

Common functions: str(), int(), float(), bool()

Pro tip: Use type() to check a variable's type — type(age) will return <class 'int'>.
objectives: Create and use variables in Python
Understand strings, integers, floats, and booleans

modules.title: Control Flow: If/Else & Loops
modules.content:
Making Decisions with If/Else

Programs need to make decisions. Python uses if, elif, and else for this:

age = 18

if age >= 18:
    print("You can vote!")
elif age >= 16:
    print("Almost there!")
else:
    print("Too young to vote.")

Important: Python uses indentation (4 spaces) to group code blocks. This is not optional — it's part of the syntax!

Comparison Operators

  • == equal to
  • != not equal to
  • >, <, >=, <= greater/less than

Loops: Repeating Things

For Loop — iterates over a sequence:

for i in range(5):
    print(f"Count: {i}")
# Output: Count: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4

While Loop — repeats while a condition is true:

count = 0
while count < 5:
    print(f"Count: {count}")
    count += 1

Practical Example

Let's calculate the total price of items in a sari-sari store order:

total = 0
items = [15, 25, 10, 30]

for price in items:
    total += price

print(f"Total: ₱{total}")  # Output: Total: ₱80
Be careful with while loops — if the condition never becomes False, your program runs forever! Always make sure the loop can end.
objectives: Write if/elif/else statements to make decisions
Create for loops and while loops

modules.title: Functions & Lists
modules.content:
What Are Functions?

Functions are reusable blocks of code. Instead of writing the same code again and again, you wrap it in a function and call it whenever you need it.

def greet(name):
    print(f"Kumusta, {name}! Welcome!")

greet("Maria")  # Kumusta, Maria! Welcome!
greet("Jose")   # Kumusta, Jose! Welcome!

The def keyword defines a function. name is a parameter — a variable the function receives.

Returning Values

Functions can also return values using the return keyword:

def add(a, b):
    return a + b

result = add(10, 20)
print(result)  # 30

Lists

Lists store multiple values in one variable:

grades = [88, 92, 75, 95, 81]
fruits = ["mango", "banana", "avocado"]

Access items by index (starting at 0):

print(grades[0])    # 88 (first item)
print(fruits[2])    # avocado (third item)
print(len(grades))  # 5 (total items)

Useful List Methods

  • .append(item) — add to end
  • .remove(item) — remove first occurrence
  • .sort() — sort the list
  • .reverse() — reverse the list

Combining Functions and Lists

def average(numbers):
    total = sum(numbers)
    return total / len(numbers)

scores = [90, 85, 78, 92, 88]
print(f"Average: {average(scores):.1f}")  # Average: 86.6
Functions are the building blocks of clean, organized code. Always try to break your problems into smaller functions!
objectives: Define and call functions with parameters
Use list methods like append, remove, and sort
Combine functions with lists for practical tasks

questions.question: Which of the following is the correct way to print text in Python?
questions.explanation: Python uses the print() function. console.log is JavaScript, echo is PHP/Shell, and System.out.println is Java.

questions.question: What is the output of: print(type(3.14))?
questions.explanation: 3.14 is a decimal number, so Python classifies it as a float. Whole numbers without decimals are integers.

questions.question:
What does the following code output?

name = "Juan"
print(f"Hello, {name}!")
questions.explanation: f-strings (formatted string literals) replace {name} with the variable's value. The f before the quote tells Python to evaluate expressions inside {}.

questions.question: Which operator checks if two values are NOT equal?
questions.explanation: In Python, != means 'not equal to'. The == operator checks equality, and <> and =! are not valid Python operators.
range(3) generates numbers 0, 1, 2. It starts at 0 and stops BEFORE the given number. This is zero-based indexing.

questions.question: How do you define a function in Python?
questions.explanation: Python uses the 'def' keyword to define functions, followed by the function name and parentheses.

questions.question: What is the index of the first element in a Python list?
questions.explanation: Python uses zero-based indexing, meaning the first element is always at index 0. This is a fundamental concept in programming.

questions.question: Which of these adds an item to the end of a list?
questions.explanation: .append() adds an item to the end of a list. .add() is for sets, .insert() adds at a specific position, and .push() is used in JavaScript arrays.
